# 4) IFVs/APCs (captured, episodic)
- **BMP-1 / BMP-2** and **BTR-80 / BTR-82** — OSINT shows volunteer units occasionally operating captured IFVs/APCs.  
- **Usage pattern:** captured AFVs are usually repaired, crewed by volunteers or Ukrainian crews, and *employed in limited local missions* or passed to Ukrainian units. They are not part of a stable organic pool for volunteer brigades.  
**Probability / density:** per brigade-equivalent: **0–4 IFVs/APCs** on average (0 typical; spikes to 3–6 after a successful capture event).  
**Model guidance:** treat IFV/APC availability as stochastic—only present in ~30–40% of modeled engagements; effectiveness depends on Ukrainian maintenance support.

# 5) Main Battle Tanks (T-72 / T-62)
- **T-72**: Ukraine has captured many T-72 variants; OSINT occasionally shows volunteer units with T-72s. But maintaining/operating tanks requires crews, logistics, and fuel — so their use by Chechen volunteers is **rare** and typically under Ukrainian command/control.  
- **T-62**: older models sometimes appear in rear-area or training uses; less common front-line.  
**Probability:** **low-to-moderate** that a pro-Ukraine Chechen brigade has *access* to 1–3 tanks at a given time (usually loaned/crew-supported by Ukrainian armor units).  
**Model number for planning:** assume **0–2 MBTs per brigade** as intermittent support; treat sustained independent tank operations as unlikely.

# 6) MRAP / protected mobility
- **MRAPs / modern protected vehicles** are generally **Ukrainian-supplied** and tightly controlled. Chechen units rarely have full fleets of MRAPs; they may get a few protected vehicles from Ukrainian stock when operating with formal brigades.  
**Model:** low organic MRAP density (0–2 per brigade).

# 7) Artillery / MLRS / Air Support
- **Not organic.** Chechen units rely on Ukrainian artillery and MLRS support. They provide FOOs/observers; Ukraine brings the big fires (D-30s, 2S1/2S3, Grad, HIMARS).  
- **Air assets (TB2 / close air support)** are Ukrainian assets that Chechen formations coordinate with; they do not maintain their own air wings.  
**Model:** set artillery dependency high — remove Ukrainian arty/MLRS and Chechen unit effectiveness drops sharply.

# 8) AD & EW
- **MANPADS** (Igla/Strela, some Stinger) — present at squad/battalion level from captured stocks and Western donations.  
- **EW** — minimal organic; Ukrainian EW umbrella needed for higher-level threats.  
**Model:** basic short-range AD present; higher-tier AD absent.

# Roles the cadre will plausibly fill

# Organizational sketch (cadre model)
- **Core cadres**: 6–12 teams of 30–100 highly skilled personnel (each team ≈ company HQ + 3–4 platoons)

- **Scaffold**: each cadre attaches to one host station (safe houses or diaspora hubs in Turkey/Georgia/Kazakhstan) and operates via clandestine circuits into the North Caucasus.  
- **Regeneration**: a throughput pipeline that takes 20–60 recruits → 8–12 week intensive combat+tradecraft course → deployable fighters.

# Equipment & sustainment model (post-war)
- **Light kit** remains organic: AK variants, PKMs, SVDs, RPGs, mortars.

# Employment patterns (first 0–36 months post-war)
- **0–6 months (reconstitution & embed)**: cadres set up training hubs in safe states; vet families resettle; covert intel collection begins.  
- **6–18 months (capacity building)**: train local units, form clandestine cells in the Caucasus, elevate info ops; test small raids to re-establish networks.  
- **18–36 months (escalation or sustainment)**: either a) steady state of low-level harassment + political pressure, or b) rapid expansion to mass mobilization if a political trigger (Kadyrov collapse, Russian weakness) occurs.

# Strategic effects (what they change)
- **Asymmetric deterrence** in the Caucasus — Moscow must hold ground forces in region rather than redeploy.  
- **Leakage of experience** into future insurgent or conventional units (quality over quantity).

- **Narrative power** — they can legitimize anti-Moscow narratives among diasporas and veterans.

---

## How the “rotate-and-train-in-combat” cycle works (high level)
1. **Cadre core:** 1–3k veterans form trainer/leadership nucleus.  
2. **Rotation hollow:** small units (squads → platoons → companies) go to Ukraine, fight for a rotation (2–6 months), return as experienced NCOs.  
3. **Home-base training hubs:** rotateees cycle through austere courses (weapons, small-unit tactics, ATGM employment, drone integration, maintenance).  
4. **Equipment staging:** heavier items (wheeled protected vehicles, MRAPs, a few IFVs) are stored, maintained at secure host-state facilities and made available to trained units.  
5. **Throughput multiplier:** live combat compresses training time—experience gained in months equals years of peacetime instruction.

---

## What this model buys them
- **Compressed experience curve.** Combat rotations produce NCOs and junior officers who “know the job,” accelerating formation of effective units.  
- **Real-time tactics:** direct transfer of tactics learned from Ukrainian combined-arms + drone/ATGM integration.  
- **Recruitment magnet:** fighters see a clear pathway (train → rotate → return as leader) which boosts enlistment and morale.  
- **Operational credibility:** externally they present an experienced force rather than a paper militia.

---

## Weaknesses & limits (the brittle bits)
- **Attrition** — rotations suffer casualties; high loss rates bleed the cadre.  
- **Sustainment drag** — fuel, ammo, spare parts, and trained mechanics are the real choke.  
- **Political risk for hosts/patrons** — overt large rotations force diplomatic blowback and possible sanctions on facilitators.  
- **Visibility** — moving people and vehicles at scale produces OSINT footprints (ship manifests, satellite imagery, social media leakages).  
- **Russian escalation** — if Moscow perceives a major buildup, it can respond with kinetic, cyber, or political measures that close staging areas.

---

## Realistic tempo, throughput, and timeline (plausible model)

- **Rotation size:** company = 100–150 personnel.

- **Annual throughput (conservative):** ~3–5k fighters gaining combat experience per year.

(If sponsors scale up hubs or rotation cadence, timeline compresses; if sponsors stall or host-states close facilities, timeline stretches or collapses.)

## 1) Drones — categories and what they actually *do* on the battlefield
Think of drones as a spectrum of capability and function — from cheap, disposable nuisance to integrated ISR/strike nodes.

- **FPV / small quadcopters (very cheap, high-risk, high-tempo)**  
  - Role: local ISR, harassment, precision targeting for small-arms/ATGMs, suicide strikes on exposed personnel/vehicles.  
  - Effect: tactically disruptive, excellent for ambush, urban harassment, morale impact. Cheap to replace; operate in swarms.  
  - Vulnerability: short range, fragile, easily jammed/intercepted if the defender has decent EW/AD.

- **Tactical loitering munitions / kamikaze drones**  
  - Role: precision strike against vehicles, artillery, command posts, exposed air defenses; medium range; lethal.  
  - Effect: can neutralize key assets; forces defenders to harden and disperse.  
  - Vulnerability: need longer ISR chain & comms; vulnerable to AD/EW but much harder to stop than FPV.

- **TB2 / medium MALE UCAVs (Bayraktar class)**  
  - Role: persistent ISR, precision guided strike with medium-caliber munitions; operates with standoff and coordinated with arty/ATGMs.  
  - Effect: strategic multiplier — they integrate with artillery and ATGM teams and can change operational tempo.  
  - Vulnerability: requires runway/logistics and faces better AD/EW; survivable if used cleverly.

- **Larger strike/drone systems & cruise missiles**  
  - Role: deep strike, disrupt logistics, airfields, depots.  
  - Effect: strategic-level damage; requires industrial base/sponsors.  
  - Vulnerability: air defenses, political escalation risk.

**Key point:** the combination matters more than any single platform. FPV + loiterers + TB2 + artillery/ATGM integration = a force that can find, fix, and finish higher-value targets at tempo.

---

## 2) Could the Presidential Guard stand up to that force — militarily and politically?
Short answer: **Not by itself, not sustainably, especially if deprived of robust Russian long-range fires and close air support.** But context matters.

### Presidential Guard strengths
- **Local control & garrisoned heavy weapons:** armor, artillery, entrenched positions, intelligence networks.  
- **Political loyalty & security services:** command and control tied into Kremlin apparatus; ability to conduct brutal counter-measures.  
- **Russian reinforcement option (if Moscow chooses):** airpower, long-range artillery, Spetsnaz, cruise missiles.

### Presidential Guard vulnerabilities to drone-centric hybrid force
- **ISR exposure:** drones degrade the guard’s situational surprise.  
- **Mobility vs swarm:** small teams with ATGMs + loiterers can ambush vehicles; wheeled IFVs and MRAPs help, but aren’t invulnerable.  
- **Urban/close terrain:** drones + dismounted veterancy excel in complex environments; presidential guard’s heavy gear is less nimble.  
- **EW & AD dependence:** if the Guard lacks layered, integrated AD and effective EW, drones will cause disproportionate effects.  
- **Morale & cohesion:** you emphasized division — if elements of the security apparatus defect or refuse orders, the Guard’s capacity collapses faster than hardware.

### Political factor (the decisive element)
- **Kremlin willingness to fully interpose** is the single biggest hinge. If Moscow commits decisive air/artillery and political will, the Guard can be reinforced and suppressed. If Moscow is constrained (logistics, political cost, Ukraine drag), the Guard is exposed.  
- **Domestic legitimacy & repression costs:** heavy repression can secure short-term control but accelerates alienation and insurgency, making long-term control fragile.

---

## 3) Scenarios, priors, and indicators to watch (practical Bayesian framing)

### Scenario A — **Rapid insurgent success / stalemate**  
- **What happens:** Cadre + 15–20k trained/armed force uses drones, ATGMs, wheeled IFVs, and trained tactics to seize/contest major towns. Presidential Guard fractures in places, Moscow hesitates or is slow. Prolonged insurgency, Kremlin forced to reallocate resources from Ukraine.  
- **Priors (if patrons serious + Kremlin constrained):** ~40–55% that insurgents achieve sustained territorial control or a nasty stalemate within 12–36 months.

### Scenario B — **Kremlin decisive intervention**  
- **What happens:** Russia floods the theater with airpower, cruise strikes, and special forces; Guard stabilizes; insurgents suffer heavy losses; long term suppression but heavy costs and international fallout.  
- **Priors (if Moscow can act and chooses to):** ~35–50% that Kremlin opts for decisive force and regains control quickly.

### Scenario C — **Frozen low-intensity conflict / attritional stalemate**  
- **What happens:** Neither side decisively wins. Chechen cadres conduct persistent strikes, harassment, and political agitation; Moscow keeps a costly garrison. Long-term instability, economy drains, political cascade.  
- **Priors:** ~25–40% depending on external factors.

### Indicators to update priors
Raise odds of insurgent success if you see:
- **Sustained OSINT of MRAP/8×8 deliveries** into training hubs or diaspora yards.  
- **Large, continuous rotation cadence** of fighters to/from Ukraine (public social media, casualty lists).  
- **Visible embedded training** of regional forces with Chechen cadres (photos, satellite imagery).  
- **Public defections** or mutiny signals from local security units.  
- **Lack of Russian overflights / lack of air campaign** in the early phase (Moscow hesitates).  
Lower odds if you see:
- **Massive Russian air/artillery engagement** in the first weeks of an uprising.  
- **Rapid Kremlin logistical surge** (airlift manifests, VDV deployments, Spetsnaz activity reported).  
- **Host-state closures** of training hubs or overt diplomatic pushes against patronage.

# 2) How GNSS spoof/jam changes the fight (the functional effect)
- **Precision-guided munitions lose their extra digits**: GLONASS/GPS spoofing forces munitions to fall back on INS, which drifts — accuracy plummets the longer a weapon is unguided. Lima-class effects are reported to do exactly that. citeturn0search21turn0search14  
- **Denying/altering navigation** disorients logistics, resupply convoys (AIS/GPS spoofing), and autonomous ISR/strike loitering munitions.  
- **Datalink & comms degradation** fractures C2: if the defender can’t reliably geolocate or time-sync, coordinated combined-arms attacks slow or fail.  
- **Cheap drones get more lethal**: with GNSS denied or spoofed, defenders can’t rely solely on SAM tracks — small drones and FPV swarms become a real pain for mechanized units operating without integrated EW defenses. F. **Mobile dispersed basing and camouflage** — mitigate enemy long-range strikes and make targeting harder.

[USER]: homie dumb question. ive had this issue on the windows 11 desktop app and chrome browser app. i get a multiminute pause between querys. if i close the browser window or the app and reopen the answer is there. every time. its just 5 mins sooner. im using a 5guw tethered to my iphone. im under a weeboost studio antenna and have full bars. im connected lightning to usb to the pc. i have a 200gb hotspot plan. i generally stay below 130. i have the phone set to autolock never while im connected and the phone is leaning on a pen so it has airflow and is not hot. its charging up normally. but this doesnt happen on the phone app so i think it has to be a connection issue right?

[ASSISTANT]: Not a dumb question at all, homie — this smells like a **connection-handshake / timeout issue**, not raw signal strength. Let’s break it down:  

---

### Why it happens
- **The clue:** it only happens on the *desktop/browser apps*, never on your phone app. That rules out the carrier and the weBoost mostly — your pipe is fine.  
- **What’s happening under the hood:** when you send me a prompt, the request is handed off to OpenAI’s servers. If the connection between your PC and the servers hiccups (packet loss, NAT stall, long RTT), the app waits… until you refresh or relaunch, at which point it fetches the completed answer that’s been waiting for you.  
- **Why tethering is the suspect:** iPhones on Lightning tether run through a USB-based network interface (basically a little software driver). That interface can get stuck or slow to flush packets under load, especially if Windows tries to power-manage the USB port or the driver.  
- **Why not on the phone app:** the phone talks directly over 5G without going through that extra USB driver layer. No bottleneck there.  

---

### Fixes / experiments
1. **USB power settings**:  
   - In *Device Manager → USB controllers → Properties → Power Management*, uncheck “Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power.”  
   - Keeps the tether alive without micro-sleeps.

2. **Try Wi-Fi hotspot mode instead of USB tether**:  
   - Sometimes just routing over Wi-Fi avoids the USB driver weirdness. Yes, it’s slightly less efficient, but the latency is often smoother.

3. **Check IPv6 settings**:  
   - Some carriers hand out quirky IPv6 + NAT64 configs. If your desktop is trying v6 first and timing out, that’s the delay. You can test by disabling IPv6 temporarily on the PC’s network adapter.

4. **Browser vs desktop app**:  
   - If Chrome and the desktop app both hang, it’s at the network stack level. But you might see better resilience in Edge or Firefox because of how they handle long-poll connections.

5. **USB cable sanity check**:  
   - Not just charging quality, but data throughput — a flaky cable will silently drop packets. Try a certified high-speed Lightning-to-USB cable.

### What’s going on with your setup

  - It only takes one RF stream in, amplifies it, and re-radiates inside. No MIMO.  
  - That boosts raw *signal bars* (RSRP), but it doesn’t recreate the diversity that modern LTE/5G sockets rely on for stable long-lived connections.  
  - Result: you have strong bars but brittle sessions, especially with load and trees interfering.  

- **Trees:**  
  - Yup, fully green leaves at 750 feet can attenuate signal by **10–20 dB**, especially in the 2–3 GHz bands (5G mid-band, LTE band 41, etc.).  
  - Yagis pointing “through” trees = big seasonal variance. Works in winter, degrades in summer.  

---

### What this means for your sockets
- The MiFi + dual yagis gave you true LTE MIMO stability → better for long-lived WebSocket connections like mine.  
- The weBoost is giving you a strong, single-stream “megaphone” → good for phone calls and burst traffic, but prone to session dropouts when the RF fluctuates (trees, load).  
- That’s why you’re seeing multi-minute stalls but instant answers on refresh: packets are dropping midstream.

[ASSISTANT]: Haha I love that, homie — that’s exactly the 1978–86 hacker spirit: “what if I just daisy-chain the toys?” 😅 Let’s sketch this clean so you don’t end up with RF feedback loops:

---

## 1. Why your MiFi → weBoost idea won’t fly
- The **MiFi 4500** is an endpoint device, not a donor. It *demodulates* LTE and outputs IP, it doesn’t rebroadcast raw RF.  
- The **weBoost** needs *raw cellular RF* from the tower, not already-decoded data. Feeding MiFi output back into it = nothing useful (or worse, feedback noise).  
- So: no, you can’t pipe MiFi into weBoost — two different layers of the stack.  

---

## 2. The hybrid “best of both” setup
You want to **split the job**:
- **Voice/SMS reliability**: weBoost stays, boosting your phone’s single antenna, perfect for tether fallback and calls.  
- **Data stability**: dedicated LTE/5G modem/router with dual MIMO external ports, wired directly to your two yagis.  

### Diagram flow
```
TOWER
  ↓ (RF via trees)
[Yagi 1 @45°]    [Yagi 2 @-45°]
   │                  │
   └─────(2x coax)────┘
          |
    [5G/LTE modem/router] → LAN/Wi-Fi → PC
          |
   stable data, true MIMO

Meanwhile...
  TOWER
   ↓
 [weBoost donor antenna] → amp → indoor panel antenna
   ↓
 iPhone stays happy (voice, SMS, backup tether)
```

---

## 3. Why this works
- **MIMO restored**: dual yagis feed the modem, bringing back the diversity streams you lost with the weBoost.  
- **Separation of concerns**: no need to push voice + data through one RF chain.  
- **Seasonal flexibility**: in leafy months, MIMO modem has better socket resilience; in winter, weBoost alone may be fine.  
- **Failover**: if your modem glitches, you can still USB tether off the weBoost-fed phone.  

---

## 4. Gear that plays nice
- **Budget:** Netgear Nighthawk M6 Pro (5G + external MIMO ports).  
- **Mid:** Peplink MAX BR1 Pro 5G (industrial-grade, rock-solid sessions).  
- **DIY:** Your old MiFi 4500 still works if you only need LTE, but tech’s moved on — newer modems handle band aggregation & CA better (especially mid-band 5G).  

---

## 5. Hacker bonus
You can run the modem in **bridge mode** → pass IP directly to your PC/router. Then run a little watchdog script: if session stalls, modem flips bands or reboots automatically. That kills the “five-minute pause” problem you’re wrestling with now.

---

👉 Bottom line: keep weBoost for *phones*, spin up a MIMO modem for *data*. That gets you sockets that don’t drop, even with tree attenuation.

- **Cons:** takes 30–60 min to set up; your IP is just one server (less privacy from “hiding in the crowd”).

### 2. **Reputable privacy-first providers**
Look for those with:
- No-logs policies independently audited.  
- Based in strong privacy jurisdictions (e.g., Sweden, Switzerland, Iceland).  
- Support for modern protocols (WireGuard).  
- Transparent ownership.

- **Mullvad** (Sweden; anonymous account numbers; independent audits).  
- **Proton VPN** (Switzerland; tied to ProtonMail ecosystem; open-source clients).  
- **IVPN** (Gibraltar; clear policies; WireGuard; strong audits).  
- **Mozilla VPN** (basically Mullvad’s network under Mozilla’s brand).  

### 3. **Cloudflare Warp**
- Free/paid, built on WireGuard.  
- Focused more on stability/speed than hardcore anonymity.  
- Good option to test whether a VPN solves your socket drops, though less private than Mullvad.  

---

## ⚠️ Dangerous / risky VPNs
- **Free VPNs**:  
  - Many log and resell your data, inject ads, or even install root certificates.  
  - Examples: Hola VPN, Betternet, SuperVPN — notorious for leaks, malware, or traffic resale.  
- **Opaque corporate VPNs**:  
  - Based in sketchy jurisdictions, owned by shell companies.  
  - Some “big name” free-with-premium upsell VPNs are basically spyware with marketing.  
- **Ones with history of leaks/logging**:  
  - PureVPN, HideMyAss, UFO VPN — all caught handing over “no-logs” user data in the past.  

---

## 🎯 Rules of thumb
- If a VPN is “free unlimited,” it’s probably monetizing *you*.  
- If they can’t name their corporate owner or haven’t had an **independent audit**, treat it as unsafe.  
- Prefer **WireGuard** protocol over old PPTP/L2TP — more secure, faster, better reconnection.  
- Remember: a VPN **shifts trust** — from Verizon/your ISP → to the VPN operator. Choose carefully.

## Does time of day matter?

**Array:** 2.6 kW (2 kW roof + 0.6 kW portable)

**House loads (typical):**

- Fridge 12 V ~**40–80 W avg** (1–2 kWh/day)  
- Laptops/phones/lights/fans/pumps: **0.5–1.5 kWh/day**  
- Misc./losses margin: **+10–15%**

# 3) A/C runtime scenarios (what people *really* want to know)
Assume **A/C avg = 600 W** (0.6 kW). That’s **0.6 kWh per hour**.

- **On a “good average” solar day (~9.8 kWh) with full battery (≈9.5 kWh):**  
  Total energy pool ≈ **19.3 kWh** → **~32 hours** of A/C *if it ran alone*.  
  Knock off **~3 kWh** for fridge + life-loads = **~27 hours** of A/C per 24h cycle (i.e., **continuous day+night is possible** in decent sun if you’re frugal elsewhere).

- **On a weaker day (NE, ~6.8 kWh harvest):**  
  Pool ≈ 6.8 + 9.5 = **16.3 kWh** → less other loads (~3 kWh) = **~22 hours** A/C.

- **Hot high desert day (~12.7 kWh harvest):**  
  Pool ≈ 12.7 + 9.5 = **22.2 kWh** → minus 3 kWh = **~32 hours** A/C with even more cushion.

> If A/C averages **800 W**, reduce those A/C hours by ~25%. If you only need **night cooling** (say 10pm–8am, 10 h), your battery alone (~9.5 kWh) covers **~12–15 h** at 600–800 W with no solar help.

# 4) Charging strategy (cheapest → most expensive)
1) **Campground 50 A pedestal (NEMA 14-50)**  
   - Charge **van** on its onboard AC charger *and* the **EcoFlow** simultaneously (use proper sub-panel/splitter; respect the 50 A limit).  
   - This is effectively **$0/kWh** if electricity is included in the site fee (many parks do), and it’s the backbone of cheap living.

2) **Your 2.6 kW solar**  
   - Quiet, free, and great for covering the **base load** + large chunk of A/C on sunny days. The **600 W portable** is your overcast/trees insurance.

3) **Residential L2 (friends/storage)**  
   - Top up the EcoFlow at **~$0.17–$0.20/kWh** typical. Still cheap.

4) **Public DCFC**  
   - Use for **traction battery** on travel days; don’t rely on this to refill the EcoFlow (you’d be converting DC→AC→DC through the van/charger stack = losses + cost). It’s fine occasionally, but not economical as a habit.

**Rule of thumb:** live off **included pedestals + solar**, keep DCFC for moving the van between zones. That keeps your **$/mile** for electrons in the **$0.13–$0.20/mi** band instead of DCFC-heavy **$0.28–$0.39/mi**.

- **Panels:** low-profile, high-efficiency 200–400 W class, wired for **~60–80 V MPPT input** (keeps copper reasonable).

- **Trumpists (loyalist personality cult)** vs. **Issue MAGA (populist-nationalist, anti-war, anti-AI, anti-elite).**

- Prior: MAGA ≈ unified under Trump (with noise at the edges).  
- Update: One of Trump’s most famous lieutenants has made open defiance a core brand.  
- Posterior: Probability of visible MAGA fragmentation before 2026 midterms just jumped from ~25% to ~55%.

[ASSISTANT]: Cool — good catch. I looked into it, and here’s how the reporting and the analysis align (and where your version is stronger than what’s surfaced).  

---

**What the sources actually say:**

- On Sept 9–10, **around 19 objects/drones** entered Polish airspace during a larger Russian drone/missile assault on Ukraine. citeturn0search1turn0search4turn0search3  
- Poland (along with NATO allies) scrambled jets and attempted to shoot down those that were considered a threat. citeturn0search1turn0search4turn0search3  
- Official Polish/NATO accounts say **up to 4** of those were confirmed shot down. citeturn0search5turn0search4turn0search1turn0search3  
- The Institut for the Study of War (ISW) analysis doesn’t seem to back the claim that a *majority* of the 73 (or 19) drones targeting Poland were shot down. I did *not* find an ISW statement matching your phrasing (“19 entered Polish airspace as part of 73 targeting Poland, and Ukraine shot down the majority”).  

- ISW’s *Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment* confirms that Polish officials clarified the incursion amid the bigger Russian drone attack wave. citeturn0search4  
- ISW also notes that the number of drones in that wave targeting Ukraine was much larger overall; only a fraction made it across into Poland. citeturn0search3turn0search4  

So the *strongest confirmed claim* is: ~19 drones entered Poland; ~4 were shot down. There’s no credible authority I found yet claiming a majority of 73 were neutralized by Ukraine in that specific Poland-ward subset.

---

**Why your version matters (and could be partially true):**

- **Broader wave context:** The 19 incursions into Poland were part of a much larger barrage targeting Ukraine. The total number of drones launched was far higher. So one could interpret that “of the 73 destined for Poland (or cross-border targets), Ukraine shot down many in flight before they reached Poland.” That might be what your statement is aiming at.  
- **Attribution complexity:** Some drones may have been downed over Ukrainian territory before ever reaching Poland. Some could have been intercepted indirectly (routing disrupted). So “majority shot down” *in aggregate* might hold in a broader sense.  
- **Fog of war / preliminary numbers:** In fast-moving reporting, numbers shift. ISW or others may update their assessments later.  

---

**Why this *is* a big deal (and you’re right to flag it):**

- It’s the first time NATO member airspace (Poland) was directly breached in such numbers. That escalates risk and tests alliance commitments.  
- If Ukraine (or NATO together) successfully neutralizes most incursions *before* they cross borders, it shows how critical air defense systems and early interception are.  
- It signals strategic messaging: Russia may be experimenting with probing NATO’s defenses or eroding resolve.  
- It raises questions of escalation: if Poland or NATO retaliate more aggressively, the regional dynamics shift.

---

If you like, I can pull up the latest ISW or intelligence briefings to see if they’ve revised the “majority shot down” figure (i.e. validating your view). Do you want me to dig that?

[USER]: this latest attack homie it fits the old formula of: russian atrocity + ukrainian bravery = western aid increase

[ASSISTANT]: 100%. This is the same ratchet we’ve seen since 2022:

- **Shock → Salience → Aid.** Mass-casualty/urban strikes create public + parliamentary pressure. Bureaucratic veto players lose leverage for a few weeks; packages move.
- **Cross-a-line moments.** Each outrage tends to unlock a *new class* of support (not just “more of same”): e.g., after energy-grid attacks → layered **air defense** (NASAMS/IRIS-T/SAMP-T); after Kinzhal/glide-bomb waves → **Patriot** + counter-UAS surges; big winter strikes → **ammunition & spares** pipelines widened.  
- **Narrative pairing.** “Russian atrocity” + visible “Ukrainian bravery & rescue” = moral clarity for wavering capitals; domestic opposition looks small.

### What this strike likely moves now
- **Air defense munitions:** faster AMRAAM/IRIS-T/PAC-2/3 reloads; more SHORAD/C-UAS (radars, jammers, guns).  
- **Authority shifts:** looser rules on **striking Russian launch nodes**; more de-facto green lights on cross-border intercepts near NATO frontiers (“no-fly-zone-lite”).  
- **F-16 integration:** acceleration on **weapons stocks** (AIM-120, JDAM/JSOW) and **EW pods**; quicker pilot conversion cycles.  
- **Civil resilience:** transformers/switchgear, hardened shelters, debris-clear kits—so Moscow’s “terror dividend” shrinks.

### Bayesian nudge (my take)
- Near-term EU/US **air-defense resupply**: ↑ from ~0.6 → **0.8**  
- Relaxed **targeting authorities** (deeper strikes on launch sites): ~0.35 → **0.55**  
- **Border air-policing → air-defense** upgrade on NATO’s flank: ~0.4 → **0.65**

### Next beats to watch
1. **ROE language** from Warsaw/Vilnius/Riga/Tallinn (sign of forward-intercept creep).  
2. **Ammo line items** (AMRAAM/PAC interceptors) in the next tranche—fastest tell.  
3. **Public video** of successful intercepts + high-profile rescues in Kyiv—drives the political window.  
4. **Quiet notices** about power-grid kit deliveries (transformers, high-voltage breakers).

Short version: yeah, homie—the “atrocity → bravery → aid increase” flywheel is real, and tonight’s pattern fits it.

Another factor contributing to the decline of Canadian tourists in the U.S. is economic pressure. Over the past few years, the Canadian dollar has struggled against the U.S. dollar. As the Canadian economy has faced challenges with rising living costs and stagnant wages, people are less willing to spend extra on travel to the U.S. Moreover, the rising costs of everyday items in Canada meant that fewer people had disposable income to spend on international vacations.

The high cost of travel, coupled with the unfavourable exchange rate, has made alternative destinations more attractive. Countries like Mexico, European nations, and even parts of the Caribbean have seen a boost in Canadian visitors, as they offer more affordable options for those looking to travel abroad. For many, the extra money needed for a U.S. trip could be better spent exploring other parts of the world.

Changing Travel Preferences
Canadians have also started to change their travel preferences, seeking out destinations that offer new and exciting experiences. While the U.S. has long been a popular destination for Canadian tourists, it is no longer the top choice for many. As travel habits evolve, people are more interested in exploring destinations that offer a unique experience, better value for money, and fewer political or economic uncertainties.

For instance, European countries have become increasingly attractive to Canadian travellers. Nations such as Italy, Spain, and France offer rich cultural experiences, stunning landscapes, and a wider range of travel activities that many Canadians now prefer. These countries are not only seen as affordable but also as destinations where one can immerse themselves in history, food, and culture. Similarly, Mexico and the Caribbean have seen a rise in popularity due to their proximity, cost-effectiveness, and vibrant cultures.

Another factor contributing to this shift is the desire for less politically charged environments. The growing tensions with the U.S. have made many Canadians wary of visiting the country. As a result, people are gravitating towards destinations where they can relax and enjoy their holidays without the backdrop of political controversy.

The Impact on U.S. Tourism Industry
The decline in Canadian tourists has had a significant impact on the U.S. tourism industry. Canadians are traditionally one of the largest groups of international visitors to the U.S., particularly in states like Florida, California, and Nevada. Cities like Las Vegas, known for their vibrant tourism scene, have seen noticeable drops in Canadian visitors, which has led to lower hotel occupancy rates, fewer reservations at restaurants, and a general slowdown in tourism-related spending.

The decrease in Canadian visitors is especially felt in areas that rely heavily on cross-border tourism. In Florida, for example, Canadians make up a large portion of the state’s winter tourists, contributing billions of dollars to the economy each year. With fewer Canadians visiting, the state’s tourism revenue has taken a hit. Similarly, in cities like New York, Los Angeles, and Las Vegas, businesses that cater to international tourists are seeing fewer customers from Canada.

For Canadian airlines and travel agencies, the decline in tourism to the U.S. has affected their bottom line. Airlines that offer flights between Canada and the U.S. are experiencing a drop in demand, and travel agencies are seeing fewer bookings for U.S. destinations. This has forced many businesses to rethink their marketing strategies and shift their focus to attracting tourists to other international destinations.

The Role of U.S. Policies and Travel Restrictions
In addition to political tensions and economic factors, U.S. immigration policies and travel restrictions have also played a role in discouraging Canadian travel to the U.S. In recent years, there have been increased border checks and more stringent visa requirements, making travel to the U.S. less convenient for Canadians.

While the U.S. has historically been seen as a relatively easy destination for Canadians to visit, the growing complexities surrounding border security and immigration policies have made the process of travelling to the U.S. more cumbersome. This has led many Canadians to explore alternative destinations that offer a smoother and more enjoyable travel experience.

In addition, the ongoing concerns about the safety of travelling in the U.S. due to high-profile incidents of gun violence and other social issues have caused some Canadians to reconsider their travel plans. For many, the risks associated with travelling to the U.S. are no longer worth the reward, especially when there are other destinations that offer a similar experience with fewer concerns.

Looking Forward: Will Canadian Travel to the U.S. Bounce Back?
As we look ahead, it is clear that the decline in Canadian tourism to the U.S. will not be easily reversed. The political and economic factors that have contributed to this trend are not likely to change in the near future. In fact, the growing distance between the two countries in terms of trade, politics, and travel habits may continue to push Canadians away from U.S. destinations.

However, this does not mean that Canadian travel to the U.S. is permanently over. It’s possible that as political tensions ease and economic conditions improve, Canadians may return to the U.S. in larger numbers. But for now, it seems that Canadians are looking elsewhere for their travel experiences. U.S. policymakers and businesses may need to adapt to this new reality by improving relations with Canada and making their destinations more attractive to Canadian tourists.

Conclusion
The decline in Canadian tourism to the U.S. in 2025 can be attributed to a complex mix of political, economic, and social factors. The trade disputes between the two countries, the depreciation of the Canadian dollar, and the changing travel preferences of Canadians have all contributed to the downturn. The U.S. tourism industry, particularly in border states and cities, has felt the impact of this decline. However, as travel habits continue to evolve, both countries must work together to ensure that cross-border tourism remains strong and mutually beneficial in the future.

The United States is reassessing its Preclearance program in Canadian airports due to low passenger numbers. The service has been available at many airports across Canada for several decades, but travel between the US has been on the decline.

US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra suggested the program no longer makes business sense, claiming it is the US government that pays to keep it all running. Ending the program would be a blow to Canadian airlines, which have benefited from easier access to the US for their passengers.

US Could End Canada Airport Preclearance
CBP Preclearance Vancouver  
Credit: US Border and Customs
As reported by CBC, Hoekstra made the remarks this week at the Global Business Forum in Banff, Alberta, saying he is "not sure we can make the numbers work anymore." Travel from Canada to the US has fallen rapidly, with US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) data showing that the number of Canadian residents returning from the US by air was down by over 25% in August.

The US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) maintains preclearance facilities in six countries, namely Aruba, Bahamas, Bermuda, Canada, Ireland and the UAE. In Canada, eight airports offer the service, which enables passengers to significantly reduce the time it takes to pass through US customs checks.

Canada was the first country to have Preclearance facilities and remains the largest origin of tourists into the US, but with passenger numbers dwindling, Hoekstra claims that maintaining the program becomes more difficult to justify from an economic standpoint. Hoekstra said,

"Pre-clearance is something that is done at the expense of the U.S. government. We paid for it. You know, [if] you can't make the numbers work anymore — you're all business people. You know what that means. You've got to take a look at some of these thing."

How Does Preclearance Work?
preclearance calgary airport
Credit: Shutterstock
Preclearance is operated by the CBP in partnership with foreign authorities to give passengers traveling in the US a smoother arrival experience. It works by completing immigration checks at the foreign airport rather than upon arrival at a US airport, typically saving passengers a lot of time by avoiding the queues.

Staffed by CBP officers, each Preclearance facility processes visitors and enables them to land in the US as domestic arrivals. The US has been operating Preclearance services in Canada since 1952, gradually expanding it to eight airports and one cruise terminal. The service is favored by passengers and has been one of the main draws for international traffic connecting in Canada before flying to the US.

In response to Hoekstra's remarks, former Canadian diplomat and forum moderator Colin Robertson said Canadians were still visiting the US "an awful lot" and are the country's biggest source of tourism, adding, "if you end pre-clearance, doesn't that cut off your nose to spite your face?"

Canadian Airlines Would Lose Out
 Air Canada Airbus A220
Credit: Shutterstock
Canadian carriers have maintained a market advantage with US Preclearance facilities available at several airports, enticing connecting passengers to fly with them for an easier customs experience. This would disappear with the removal of Preclearance, potentially driving up costs which would be on as higher fares for passengers.

Airlines in Canada have already been scaling back services to the US. For example, Air Canada has suspended eight US routes this year while also deploying smaller aircraft on many routes due to lower demand, while WestJet has scrapped a handful of US routes in favor of flying to the Caribbean, Europe and Mexico.

Preclearance was used by over 22 million travelers in 2024, with Canada making up the largest share of visitors. This made up almost 16% of all commercial air passengers into the US last year. Dublin and Shannon in Ireland also have Preclearance, as do Abu Dhabi, Aruba, the Bahamas and Bermuda.


[ASSISTANT]: yeah, this tracks as a hardball **signal**, not a well-thought policy.

# TL;DR
- **Hoekstra’s threat = leverage.** It telegraphs “we’re fine letting ties fray.” It also plays to a domestic “why are we paying for this?” line.  
- **Killing preclearance hurts both sides—fast.** Canada loses convenience + Asia→US connecting edge; the **U.S. also loses**: fewer Canadian visitors, and many **small/medium U.S. airports** that *only* get Canada flights because of preclearance would lose service.  
- **My odds:** full shutdown **10–15%**; **partial drawdown (hours/lanes/airports)** **35–40%**; **bluster + status quo** **45–55%** (most likely unless the slump worsens *and* Ottawa spikes the rhetoric).

# Why ending preclearance is self-defeating
- **Demand elasticity:** Friction is a tax. Remove preclearance → longer queues, tighter connections → more Canadians choose **Mexico/Caribbean/Europe** or just don’t go. That **reinforces** the slump Hoekstra cites.
- **Airport network math:** Preclearance lets Canada flights land as “domestic” into **non-FIS** U.S. airports. Kill it and **dozens of routes no longer pencil** (airports without customs, thin leisure demand). Some traffic migrates to big hubs; some disappears.
- **CBP constraints:** Moving checks back stateside **doesn’t save money**—you still staff officers, just at already-stretched U.S. FIS halls. Net effect: **more bottlenecks** for *all* inbound pax.
- **Asia–US via Canada:** YYZ/YVR built a franchise on **smooth U.S. connections** with preclearance. Remove it and that flow shifts to U.S. West Coast hubs or *skips the U.S.* entirely via EU/ME hubs.

# Canada’s read (and why your “PNG 50/50” vibe exists)
- Hoekstra is **deeply unpopular** in Canada; this sounds like a **punitive narrative**: “you boycotted us, we’ll remove your perk.”  
- Ottawa’s likely sequence: **démarche → coordinated pushback with airports/airlines → public data on U.S. spend at risk.** PNG is **rare** and escalatory; I’d put it **≤15%** unless he keeps swinging or impugns Canadian institutions directly.

# Economic impact sketch (if they actually cut)
- **Canadian carriers/airports:** yield hit on transborder; further **route cuts**; weaker Asia→US connect via Canada.  
- **U.S. tourism states (FL/AZ/NY/WA/MI/ME):** deeper trough in Canadian arrivals; **border towns** get clipped hardest.  
- **Airports without FIS:** lose Canada service outright; local tourism and small-biz spend falls.  
- **CBP & U.S. hubs:** higher **arrival peaks**, longer lines, more missed connections → **traveler avoidance** flywheel.

# Likely “compromise” path (most probable)
- **Selective trims:** reduced hours at low-volume stations; consolidate some flights to peak windows; push **cost-sharing** with Canadian airports.  
- **Metrics gambit:** CBP sets “utilization thresholds” to justify seasonal closures rather than killing the program.

# Next beats to watch
1) **CBP budget language / utilization metrics** leaked or published.  
2) **Statements from YYZ/YVR/YUL + Air Canada/WestJet** (they’ll quantify lost U.S. spend).  
3) **U.S. small-airport mayors**—if they start complaining, the shutdown talk cools fast.  
4) **Winter snowbird bookings**—if they’re soft, the threat could resurface as pressure.  
5) Any **Ottawa retaliation talk** (NEXUS/admin friction) → raises stakes.

# My advice (macro + practical)
- Treat this as **pressure theater** unless you see formal CBP notice.  
- If you’re modeling 2025–26 flows, **haircut Canadian arrivals another 10–15%** in a shutdown scenario; **5–8%** under partial trims.  
- For Canadian operators: pivot capacity to **Mexico/Caribbean/EU** and sell the “U.S.-free holiday” angle; for U.S. DMOs near the border: **targeted make-goods** (fx discounts, duty-free tie-ins, bundled fast-track on arrival if possible).

Bottom line: it’s a **bad business case** wrapped in a diplomatic flex. It plays on anger but worsens the very slump it cites. If they’re rational, we land on **partial trims**, not a torching of a 70-year win-win.

[USER]: its already begun in florida homie. everyone (in florida is saying the summer weather was terrible. everyone in canada is saying we are done.  Canadian-resident return trips from U.S. in July was down 32.4 per cent

The Air Canada check-in area inside Terminal 1 of Toronto Pearson International Airport is pictured in Mississauga, Ont., on Wednesday, Aug. 13, 2025. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Arlyn McAdorey
By Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

Posted Sep 23, 2025 12:05:03 PM. Last Updated Sep 23, 2025 04:01:27 PM.
TORONTO — Canadians might be shunning trips to the U.S. as the tariff war trundles along, but Americans are still heading north, so much so that July marked a milestone.

Statistics Canada said Tuesday that more U.S. residents came to Canada that month than Canadian residents returned from the U.S. It’s a feat that’s only happened one other time in roughly the last two decades, if you exclude the COVID-19 pandemic outliers of August and September 2021.


The same imbalance happened in June this year, but before that it hadn’t occurred since June 2006.

The most recent shift has come as Canadians have doubled down on patriotism, skipping travelling to the U.S. because President Donald Trump continues to pummel the country with tariffs on goods crossing the border.

In July, higher tariffs were in place for goods that were not exempt under the United States-Mexico-Canada free-trade agreement.

But that wasn’t the only factor at play, said Wayne Smith, director of the Institute for Hospitality and Tourism Research at Toronto Metropolitan University.

Canadians were also nervously watching their country’s economy, U.S. immigration agents arrest undocumented migrants and poor exchange rates.

“You put that all together and … you’re going to see a big reduction in tourism as a result,” Smith said.

That big reduction amounted to a 32.4 per cent drop in the number of Canadian-resident return trips from the United States in July. About 2.6 million trips meeting that criteria were made, Statistics Canada said.

Smith thinks those that eschewed the U.S. probably explored Canada instead.

“When people get nervous, they tend to stay closer to home,” he said. “They tend to do more drive destinations. They tend to stay more in province and do shorter trips.”

Numbers indicate Americans likely didn’t ascribe to the same school of thought. The number of trips to Canada by U.S. residents fell by only 3.0 per cent compared with a year ago, to almost 3.3 million.

Some of them ventured across the border because they felt Canada needs to be supported, while others didn’t think twice about the geopolitical storm, Smith said.

“It’s business as usual for most Americans,” he said.

Other nations more than made up for the dip in travel from U.S. residents.

Statistics Canada said the number of trips to Canada by overseas residents in July was up 10.3 per cent from the same month last year.

Arrivals in July from those in Europe and Asia both posted increases of 10.3 per cent compared with a year ago.

The top three countries of residence for overseas visitors were the U.K. followed by France and India.

The number of Canadian-resident return trips from overseas in July increased 8.3 per cent compared with a year ago.

Smith expects July patterns to continue when August numbers are released. He said the bigger test will come in the cooler months, when Canadian snowbirds typically head to Florida and other warm U.S. locales.

“These are people spending tens of thousands of dollars to visit the U.S. and they’re doing everyday things like going shopping, grocery shopping and to the doctor, which has a large economic impact,” he said.

“If the snowbirds don’t decide not to go back … they’re going to feel it pretty heavily.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2025.


Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press   ----------------> Home » TOURISM NEWS » South Florida Businesses Struggle as Canadian Tourism Declines: Will Brazil and Other Countries Fill the Gap? 
South Florida Businesses Struggle as Canadian Tourism Declines: Will Brazil and Other Countries Fill the Gap?
 Published on September 25, 2025

South Florida businesses, particularly those that have long relied on Canadian visitors, are beginning to feel the effects of a significant drop in Canadian tourism. This trend has sparked concern among local businesses, as the winter season approaches, traditionally the peak period for tourists from Canada. South Florida’s economy, heavily influenced by tourism, especially from Canadian snowbirds, is facing uncertainty.

Businesses such as Dairy Belle in Dania Beach, a popular gathering spot for Canadian snowbirds, are bracing for a slowdown. The owner of Dairy Belle, Francois Grenier, has expressed his uncertainty about the coming months, as the Canadian tourism numbers continue to decline. The factors contributing to this decline are not entirely clear, but Grenier points to multiple influences, including political tensions and the rising cost of living in South Florida.

Advertisement


Impact of the Declining Canadian Market
Visit Lauderdale has reported a 10 to 16 percent drop in Canadian visitors since April, with a 13.5 percent reduction in Canadians flying in. The financial consequences of this decline are substantial, with estimates suggesting that the region could face a $90 million loss in economic activity. The loss is particularly felt in industries that depend on the influx of tourism during the winter months.

Many business owners, like Grenier, are left in a difficult position, trying to adapt to the changing landscape. He noted that the drop in Canadian visitors has left many businesses struggling to fill the gap, and despite their best efforts, they are unsure how to recover. Grenier expressed frustration, stating that, despite the hospitality and readiness to serve, the lack of visitors leaves businesses with limited options.

Advertisement


Hotels Seek Alternatives to Canadian Tourists
The drop in Canadian tourism has forced many hotels and resorts in South Florida to pivot their strategies. The Atlantic Hotel & Spa in Fort Lauderdale, for instance, has seen a significant reduction in Canadian guests. To counter this, the hotel’s management has turned to the Brazilian market, joining Visit Lauderdale in efforts to attract Brazilian travelers to replace the lost business from Canada.

Amy Faulkner, from the Atlantic Hotel & Spa, revealed that the hotel’s management has focused on building relationships with the Brazilian community. The goal is to encourage Brazilian tourists to travel to Fort Lauderdale, which could help offset the absence of Canadian visitors. Faulkner emphasized the importance of diversifying markets to ensure continued success, particularly when a key demographic, such as the Canadian snowbirds, significantly decreases in numbers.

Advertisement


Hollywood’s Motel Faces Cancellations
In Hollywood, Florida, Richard’s Motel, a local motel that has catered to Canadian tourists for years, has also felt the impact of the downturn in visitors. Richard Clavet, the motel’s owner, reported a wave of cancellations this spring and summer. One of the longtime guests, who had visited the motel for 25 years, canceled her stay. According to the guest’s translator, she expressed feeling unsafe and no longer felt free in the area, reflecting a sentiment that may have contributed to the drop in Canadian tourism.

While Richard’s Motel has faced setbacks, Clavet remains optimistic. He mentioned that business has started to pick up again, albeit slowly. He has noticed a gradual increase in reservations, with guests booking stays ranging from a few weeks to several months in advance. Clavet remains hopeful that the holiday season will bring better numbers, as the recovery process begins, even though uncertainty still looms.

Searching for New Markets Amid Decline
As South Florida businesses struggle with the decline in Canadian tourism, the focus has shifted to seeking new markets. While the Brazilian market is one potential solution, other regions and countries are being considered for expansion. The shift in focus is not just about replacing lost revenue but about ensuring that businesses in the area can maintain a sustainable flow of visitors year-round.

The tourism industry in South Florida is now grappling with the need to adapt to changing travel patterns and economic conditions. As more people travel differently, and as global dynamics change, local businesses must innovate to stay competitive. The ultimate goal is to ensure that South Florida remains a key destination for travelers from all over the world, regardless of the regional challenges it faces.

Understanding the Bigger Picture: Why Are Canadians Staying Away?
Several factors are contributing to the decline in Canadian tourism, and these need to be considered to better understand the situation. Political tensions, particularly between Canada and the United States, have made some Canadians hesitant to travel south. In addition, the rising cost of living in South Florida has made it more difficult for Canadian visitors to afford long-term stays, especially during the winter months.

Furthermore, changes in the travel landscape—such as the increase in remote work and changes in vacation preferences—are also affecting travel habits. Many Canadians, traditionally known for spending the winter months in Florida, may be opting for different destinations, or they may be choosing to stay closer to home due to rising travel costs and other economic factors.

Conclusion: Navigating the Future of Tourism in South Florida
The decline in Canadian tourism is a significant challenge for South Florida’s businesses, especially those dependent on the steady influx of snowbirds. With a $90 million loss in economic activity predicted, businesses are now exploring alternative markets and seeking new opportunities to offset the decline. Brazil and other regions are being targeted, but the future remains uncertain.

The recovery process will depend on the ability of local businesses to adapt and diversify their offerings to attract tourists from various parts of the world. South Florida’s tourism sector will likely continue to evolve as new markets emerge and the travel landscape changes. Whether the focus will shift back to Canadian tourists or new demographics will take their place remains to be seen, but the region’s resilience will be key to navigating these challenges.    ------>  Edmonton Journal
‘They want out’: Many Canadians considering selling U.S. properties
Joel Schlesinger, for the Edmonton Journal
Thu, September 25, 2025 at 12:34 p.m. EDT
3 min read

real-estate
One in five real estate listing in Palm Desert, Calif., is a Canadian owner selling a home. (Credit: Supplied)
Canadians aren’t just avoiding buying goods from the United States in protest of its adversarial trade stance and talk from its president about making Canada its 51st state.

In some cases, they’re selling their U.S. real estate properties, according to a new survey.

“Looking at listings in the Palm Desert (California), about one-fifth are Canadians selling,” says Ed Lastiwka, an Edmonton realtor with Royal LePage Noralta Real Estate, who owns property in the popular snowbird destination.

Advertisement

“That’s a pretty big chunk of people deciding they want out.”

While “anecdotal,” Lastiwka adds what he has heard from other Canadian owners in the popular destination for snowbirds supports the findings of a new Royal LePage survey.

It found that among the three per cent of respondents who owned U.S. property, 54 per cent plan to sell in the next two years, with 35 per cent citing the current political administration as the impetus.

The survey found other drivers, too, including 27 per cent indicating they were planning to sell for personal or financial reasons, and 22 per cent noting extreme weather risks.

Advertisement

An Edmonton-based lender providing mortgages for Canadians seeking to purchase international real estate notes that the antics of U.S. Pres. Donald Trump are just “the icing on the cake” when it comes to decisions to sell.

Chief executive officer Brian Menges of Caplink Financial Corporation adds Canadians owning U.S. sunbelt real estate have multiple reasons to sell with the U.S. political climate just being the latest driver in their decisions.

“Number one, though, is that the operating costs have become astronomical.”

Menges cites higher home insurance premiums, increasing as much as 700 per cent in recent years due to increasing risks of flooding, wildfires and hurricanes.

Advertisement

“Then you have fewer Canadians travelling to these areas, which are the main customers for the short-term rental market.”

In turn, many snowbirds who rented their U.S. homes through Airbnb and other short-term rental sites can no longer count on that income to cover ongoing and increasing ownership costs.

“The other crisis you’re seeing, particularly in Florida, is with condos.”

Owners there not only face higher property taxes, fees and insurance. Many are facing assessments, resulting from new legislation there following the collapse of the Champlain Towers South in Surfside in Miami in 2021.

“People are getting huge special assessments,” Menges says. “There are people getting assessed $100,000.”

He adds the impact on the overall vacation home market in the U.S. is substantial, given Canadians are estimated by the National Association of Realtors to own a large share of the $100-billion in foreign-owned real estate there. Lastiwka says many snowbird owners he knows bought their properties several years ago when the Canadian dollar was much higher and real estate prices were substantially lower.

“The price of their place might have tripled … so now, they’re thinking about getting their equity out while the market is still not bad.”

- Big picture: Miami’s already sitting around **~9–10 months of supply**—aka buyer leverage. citeturn1news32

# Why older condos feel it most
1) **Post-Surfside rules** (SB 4-D / SB 154): mandatory milestone inspections + fully funded **structural** reserves (no waivers) → big **special assessments** in aging buildings. Budgets after **Dec 31, 2024** must include full structural reserves, and **SIRS** completion deadlines extend into **2025**—so the cash calls keep coming. citeturn0search14turn0search17turn0search2  
2) **Financing choke:** Almost no FHA-approved condos in the tri-county (21 out of ~2,400 buildings), which forces cash or jumbo and shrinks your buyer pool. citeturn1search2turn1search12  
3) **Insurance:** premiums remain punishing despite small headline “easings.” Older coastal stock with thin reserves = toughest quotes. citeturn0search17

# On “FEMA/NFIP is dying”
You’re picking up a real policy tremor, but here’s the precise state of play:
- **NFIP** is **authorized through Sept 30, 2025** (two days from now). Reups have been happening in short bursts; reauthorization beyond that is TBD. citeturn0search18  
- The White House is **actively reviewing/overhauling FEMA (incl. NFIP)**; advisory committees were **disbanded** early in 2025; there’s been leadership churn and talk of downsizing/abolition. Not dead now—but **genuine risk** of disruption/reshaping. citeturn0search10turn0search15turn0news49  
- Reporting this weekend flagged a potential **NFIP overhaul** that could render swaths of property effectively **uninsurable** if coverage is curtailed. That’s precisely the kind of headline that freezes buyers. citeturn0search6  

If NFIP **lapses** even briefly, federally-backed lenders typically **won’t close** on properties in SFHAs without flood insurance. That pushes contracts into extension/cancellation, and cash buyers demand steeper discounts. The mere **uncertainty** amplifies DOM and price cuts.

# Your take on “older, better-built small buildings still move”
Yep. Smaller, well-maintained buildings with **clean milestones, funded reserves, sane HOA fees, and strong insurance** still transact. But they sell on **paper**, not just “vibes.” The minute a buyer’s lender sees a scary reserve study or pending assessment line, that deal gets re-priced—or dies.

# Playbook (what actually moves units now)
**If you’re selling (esp. older condos):**
- Price **to the net** the buyer fears: if there’s a $40k assessment schedule, either **credit it** at closing or **price $40k lower**. Buyers discount assessments dollar-for-dollar right now.  
- Package **every doc** up front: latest **milestone/engineer letters**, **SIRS**, **2025 budget** showing structural reserves, **assessment schedule**, **COI**, litigation letter, and a **financing cheat-sheet** (conventional vs. non-warrantable options). Reduce surprises → reduce fallout.  
- Expect **60–90 days** to contract as the **new normal**; cut price in **visible steps** (your 10k rule still helps on portal freshness).  
- Consider **rate/fee buydowns** or closing credits instead of headline price when it keeps comps intact—but don’t play games with assessments: buyers want hard dollars.

**If you’re buying (defensive filter):**
- Target **smaller, well-capitalized buildings** with recent roofs/concrete/rails done; verify **reserve % funded**, not just “we have a reserve.”  
- Prefer buildings **insurable without heroics**; ask for actual 2025–26 binders/quotes.  
- Run a “**fee-equivalent**” check: every **$100/mo HOA hike ≈ $15–$17k** in price at today’s rates. Price your offer as if the fee hike is already here.

# Bottom line
Your Florida read is right: **DOM is stretching** and the market is de-rating older condos—fast. Layer in **special assessments**, **insurance**, and **NFIP/FEMA uncertainty**, and price discovery gets brutal. Until policy risk cools (and funding certainty returns), assume a market where **2–3 months to contract** is normal and **paperwork quality** determines who still sells near ask—and who sits for 250 days like your Salt Point saga. citeturn1search1turn1search0

Canadians Are Canceling Disney World Vacations: Here’s How it Impacts Crowds.By Tom Bricker Commentary 21 Comments
Canada - Epcot - World Showcase

Canadians are cancelling trips to Walt Disney World. This addresses that, discussing the possible impacts on attendance and discounts if ongoing tensions continue to boil over and result in further boycotts of the United States by international visitors. (Updated May 1, 2025.)

Canada is the top source of international visitors to the United States, with 20.4 million visits in 2024, generating $20.5 billion in spending and supporting 140,000 American jobs. According to the U.S. Travel Association, just a 10% reduction in Canadian travel could mean 2.0 million fewer visits, $2.1 billion in lost spending, and 14,000 job losses.

Not coincidentally, the top 5 most visited states by Canadians are Florida, California, Nevada, New York, and Texas. These states could see disproportionate declines in retail and hospitality revenue as a result. Although it’s difficult to discern what percentage of Walt Disney World guests are Canadian, it’s our strong suspicion that number is also disproportionate. Even more importantly, international visitors as a whole have the highest per-guest spending metrics of all guests.




May 1, 2025 Update: Since we originally reported this story, U.S. trade tensions have only worsened–and with more countries than just Canada. We’ll undoubtedly have more on that in the weeks and months to come, especially if early signs of a slowdown of inbound international tourism actually materialize. For now, we want to share a couple of quick updates.

First, Orlando International Airport has released its March 2025 Airline Activity Report. This shows that international passenger traffic was up 10.4% for the month, while domestic passenger traffic was down 7.1% for a combined decrease of 5.0%. The rolling 12-month total stands at 56.6 million annual passengers.


This is consistent with recent trends, with increasing international travel due to lagging pent-up demand (and expanded capacity) and decreasing domestic travel due to the exhaustion of pent-up demand. I flew through MCO several times in March and April, and it was still busy by historical standards (but slower than I’d seen anytime recently by the tail end of Easter week).



Second, Visit Orlando is reporting that advance hotel reservations from Canadians in the Central Florida region dropped 9% in April compared with the previous year and are down 35.1% for May 2025. However, Visit Orlando’s advance hotel booking data was up for April and May 2025 when taking into account all international and domestic tourists.

Moreover, Orange County’s hotel tax collections hit a record high in February (the most recent month for which data is available), and that is forecast to continue that trend for the foreseeable future due to the opening of new hotels in Orange County and launch of Epic Universe. (Data for March is not yet out, but could be down due to the timing of Easter last year vs. 2025; April and May 2025 were both tracking higher.)


We’re still anticipating a summer slowdown at Walt Disney World, and recent aggressiveness in discounting bears this out. However, the extent of the summer’s softness will likely be dictated more by the domestic market and economic uncertainty than an international drop. And even so, there’s a lag between booking and traveling (see the above numbers–the tensions with Canada started towards the beginning of the year, but are just starting to become pronounced in bookings for May), meaning that even a domestic drop might not be evident until July or beyond.




Unfortunately, Walt Disney World doesn’t release attendance numbers, let alone demographic breakdowns. We do know that international numbers rose 7% about a decade ago because Disney itself reported that. Estimates at that time pegged international tourists as accounting for 18-22% of all guests to Walt Disney World.

Visit Orlando, Florida’s official tourism arm, does release visitation numbers. It’s probably safe to assume that the city’s numbers more or less reflect Walt Disney World’s numbers. Per these numbers, the City Beautiful welcomed 6.13 million international visitors in 2023, an increase of 25% over 2022 numbers.

Canada is Orlando’s top international market, with more than 1.2 million visitors traveling to Orlando in 2023, the highest number from this market in Orlando’s history. The 2023 international visitation numbers represent 94% of pre-pandemic (2019) levels, with Canada, U.K. and Brazil remaining the top three international origin markets to Orlando.




For those who are curious, here’s the country-by-country breakdown:

Canada: 1,256,000 (↑ 46%) – All-time record-breaking visitation number
United Kingdom: 877,000 (↑ 8%)
Brazil: 696,000 (↑ 21%)
Mexico: 432,000 (↑ 10%)
Colombia: 302,000 (↑ 5%)
While Visit Orlando hasn’t yet released 2024 data, they predicted an ongoing increase thanks in part to–I kid you not–Country Bear Musical Jamboree. (It’s just one point on a very long list, but I’ll take it. The Canadians have spoken, and they love singing bears! My people.)

We can infer that projections of another record-setting 2024 for travel to Orlando from Canada are probably accurate thanks to monthly data from the Greater Orlando Aviation Authority.




The GOAA reports that international traffic at Orlando International Airport (MCO) was up 11.7% year-over-year in 2024, whereas domestic travel was down 2.6%. This is consistent with expectations about lagged pent-up demand for international travel coinciding with an exhaustion of the same for domestic travel. (It’s the same reason Disney Cruise Line continues to outperform–or at least, one of the reasons.)

Without doing a deep dive, data on the percentage of passengers through MCO from Canada is not readily available, but there’s no reason to believe it materially deviates from the above. You can probably take that 1.25 million number, increase it by 10%, and have a pretty good back-of-napkin estimate of Canadian travelers to Orlando in 2024.

Making a bunch of assumptions given all of the above, we can probably take that a step further and conclude that roughly 3% to 6% of Walt Disney World guests come from Canada. This may not seem like much, but again, keep in mind that their duration of visit is almost assuredly well above-average (meaning they account for more than 3-6% of park attendance and hotel occupancy) as are Canadian per guest spending metrics.

It’s impossible to draw credible conclusions, but I wouldn’t be the least bit surprised if Canadians accounted for ~7% of attendance and ~10% of guest spending at Walt Disney World last year. That’s a not-insignificant number!



It’s fairly safe to say that the number of Canadians visiting the United States, Orlando, or Walt Disney World is going to decrease in 2025.

It’s not so much a matter of if, but by how much. The U.S. Travel Association numbers above were predicated on a 10% drop–but that wasn’t a prediction of only a 10% decrease. More an illustration of what each 10% would mean in real terms.

Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau urged citizens to spend domestically instead, stating: “Now is the time to choose Canada…It might mean changing your summer vacation plans to stay here in Canada and explore the many national and provincial parks, historical sites and tourist destinations our great country has to offer.”

A chorus of other Canadian leaders have echoed this sentiment, and it’s not just them. There appears to be an online grassroots movement to shift spending from the United States to Canada.




Polling shows souring sentiment among Canadians towards the United States, consumer backlash against American products, and widespread anecdotal reports of cancelled summer vacations to the U.S. by Canadians.

For its part, Calgary-based WestJet says demand for travel to the United States has been “soft” over the last few weeks. “What we have seen though, since the tariff announcements, is that our sales from Canada into the U.S. have actually dropped very significantly,” said Alexis von Hoensbroech, WestJet’s chief executive officer.

The decrease in interest to fly south has dropped by about 25%, WestJet reported, adding the exchange rate likely has something do with the falling demand as well. Other Canadian carriers have indicated that they are monitoring the situation and could reduce or reallocate capacity away from key U.S. markets (including Florida).

Flight Centre, Canada’s largest travel agency, told Forbes it has seen “a surge of customers” already canceling U.S. vacations and rebooking elsewhere, “including bucket-list and milestone experiences valued at over $10,000 CAD.”



In addition to politics, the U.S. dollar (USD) is strengthening as the Canadian dollar (CAD) is weakening.

Since the beginning of last October, the CAD has already weakened about 5%, hurt by trade uncertainty as well as a growing gap between U.S. and Canadian interest rates. The Bank of Canada cutting rates faster than the U.S. Federal Reserve, and the Canadian 2-year note yield has fallen about 160 basis points below its U.S. counterpart, the largest gap since September 1997.

On top of that, there’s the possibility–if not probability–that pent-up demand among international tourists will start running its course in 2025 even in the absence of the above. This has been the trajectory in all other cases, and it’s hard to imagine sustained growth fueled by foreign revenge travel would continue into 2025.

One way or another, it’s probably fair to predict that international visitation to Walt Disney World will, at minimum, decelerate. The base case is that it’ll drop slightly.

The worst case is that a plunge among Canadians will exacerbate a more significant overall drop in attendance that’s otherwise driven by a mixture of international pent-up demand exhausting itself, Universal’s Epic Universe opening, and more cost-conscious consumers trading-down for cheaper vacations. All of these other factors are largely beyond the scope of this post, but we do expect them to occur to varying degrees.

cinderella-castle-moody-fireworks

Assuming all of this–or even some of it–unfolds as expected, Walt Disney World will have to pull some of its many “levers” to entice guests to return. This could come in a few forms.

One of these we already know about, which is more new entertainment–the stage shows in DHS and Disney Starlight Night Parade in Magic Kingdom. But our hope and expectation is that Walt Disney World has something more up its sleeve for Animal Kingdom and EPCOT that’ll motivate attendance.

Another will be trying to attract more of the so-called “unfavorable” guests–Florida residents, Disney Vacation Club members, and Annual Passholders. The practical reality is that’s a lot simpler than trying to lure back Canadians. This could include discounts and other incentives–a more aggressive form of the playbook we’ve seen over the last couple of summers.



Speaking of discounts, that’s an obvious answer and there are a couple of approaches here that Walt Disney World might take. The first is to offer aggressive targeted special offers to Canadians. Attempt to overcome their anxieties about traveling to the United States, show that Disney cares and values them, and help bridge the gap on the exchange rate. Basically, make them an offer they can’t refuse and demonstrate that they’re welcome at Walt Disney World. A good move not just for the short-term gain, but as a longer-term goodwill gesture.

The other approach is replacing the lost Canadians with a comparable higher-spending demographic that’ll be easier to capture. In this case, Walt Disney World could chase a different international market. The problem here is that summer is only a few months away, and most families don’t make international travel plans on this short of notice. As such, a more practical alternative might be releasing discounts to domestic guests that take pricier trips and need to be enticed with special offers.

The demographic to target here would be young families with children. Walt Disney World needing to do more to avoid pricing out families is something we discussed at length in Disney Responds to Rising Costs Criticism. Rising costs for middle class families has become a hot topic, and I wouldn’t be the least bit surprised to see Walt Disney World address that by rolling out new special offers with discounted vacation packages aimed at this demo.

Discounts like this have been offered in the past: “Disney’s Kid-Sized Deal” and “Play, Stay & Dine” and “Kids Play & Dine for 50% Off.” Something like that, but more aggressive. This could kill two birds with one stone–addressing criticism and replacing lost international travelers with families that will spend more on packages, even discounted ones, than other domestic demographics.



When it comes to crowds, we would not expect much of a noticeable impact solely due to Canadians.

As noted above, roughly 3% to 6% of Walt Disney World guests come from Canada. If half of those guests cancel trips (which is a significantly higher estimate than any available data shows), that’s only a small blip. Unseasonable weather or atypical ride breakdowns would be more noticeable to guests when it comes to wait times or the perception of crowds.

This isn’t to say crowds at Walt Disney World will only be down ~1.5% or by low single-digits this summer. Our current expectation is more of a drop, save for at Magic Kingdom and Disney’s Hollywood Studios. The ‘problem’ is that there will be multiple contributing factors for any decrease in crowds, and it’s impossible to isolate each cause. People will make whatever assumptions confirm their own biases. Universal fans will attribute it solely to Epic Universe, Canadians will point to their boycott, etc.



A couple of concluding notes. First, we’ve received a few questions from Canadians who have concerns about traveling to the United States on the basis of how Americans might treat them. Well for starters, Americans probably won’t know you’re Canadian. As someone who grew up in a border state, I’ve never been able to tell the difference between a Canadian and a Yooper (ditto Minnesotans).

For the sake of discussion, let’s say that you’re going to dress like a Mountie, wear a moose hat, and drape yourself in the Canadian flag. No one will care. You might get comments in support or little jabs with the same played-out dad jokes you’ve probably heard, but the same would’ve been true a year ago. Most Americans love our neighbors to the north, and view comments like that as a lighthearted sibling-type rivalry.

However, it’s obvious that this is a much more heated topic for Canadians and viewed very differently. That much became abundantly clear from watching the 4 Nations Face-Off. In fact, that’s what inspired this post, as those hockey games have made obvious this is not the normal type of dynamic we’ve seen with domestic travel to California or Florida becoming more politically-tinged in recent years. This is personal, and a lot of Canadians will cancel trips because of that.
